title: Option in Functions
story: You're writing a math library. Division by zero is the enemy — it crashes programs. Instead of letting it happen, your function needs to say 'I can't do that' without exploding. Option to the rescue!
why: Functions that return Option[T] explicitly signal that they might fail — callers must handle the 'nothing' case, making code safer by design.
analogy: A function returning Option is like a vending machine — you put in money and press a button. If the item is in stock, it drops (Some). If it's sold out, nothing comes out (None).
try_it: Write a `safe_average(a, b, c)` function that returns Option[Int]. Return None if the sum is 0 (to avoid a trivial average). Otherwise return Some(sum / 3). Test with all positive, all zero, and mixed values.
tips: Return `None` early when validation fails — this keeps the happy path clean at the bottom
The return type `Option[Int]` documents that callers must handle the 'no result' case
Use `.unwrap_or()` at the call site if you have a good default — but match when you need different logic per case
common_mistakes: Returning `None` from a function whose signature says `-> Int` — the return type must be `-> Option[Int]`
Wrapping everything in Some without checking conditions — defeats the purpose of Option
Forgetting that `a / b` when b is 0 crashes even inside a function returning Option — you must check BEFORE dividing
